level: serious amateur aiming at professional competence

schools.name: Scientific school
schools.optimises_for: music as a measurable object — systematic transcription, controlled comparison, and hypothesis-testing (comparative musicology, Lomax's cantometrics)
schools.gives_up: the lived meaning of the music for the people who make it

schools.name: Interpretive school
schools.optimises_for: music as culture — meaning, emic perspective, and thick description (Merriam's 'music in culture', Geertz)
schools.gives_up: cross-cultural comparability — each tradition is read on its own terms

schools.name: Applied school
schools.optimises_for: reciprocity and impact — community collaboration, repatriation, and public scholarship that returns value to the community
schools.gives_up: detached neutrality — the researcher takes sides and shares control of the work

schools.name: Documentary school
schools.optimises_for: capturing and preserving recordings as cultural heritage — durable, documented, and archived for future generations
schools.gives_up: analysis depth — the recording matters more than the interpretation

clusters.name: Discipline & questions
clusters.gist: What ethnomusicology studies, its history, and its recurring debates — the questions that define the field before any recording is made.

clusters.name: Fieldwork & documentation
clusters.gist: Preparation, ethics of access, recording technique, interviews, participant observation, field notes — the evidence-gathering core of the discipline.

clusters.name: Transcription & notation
clusters.gist: Notating recorded music — Western notation, LAB shorthand, graphical systems, rhythm and tuning — and knowing what notation cannot capture.

clusters.name: Musical & cultural analysis
clusters.gist: Formal analysis of the music — form, scale, rhythm, timbre — plus cultural interpretation and comparison across traditions.

clusters.name: Ethnographic writing
clusters.gist: The written account — thick description, reflexivity, voice, structure, and the venues that publish it.

clusters.name: Ethics & community
clusters.gist: Informed consent, IRB, intellectual property, repatriation, collaboration, ownership — the obligations that fieldwork carries.

clusters.name: Recording stewardship & archiving
clusters.gist: Metadata, file standards, preservation, deposit into archives, and return of recordings to the communities that made them.

nodes.label: Discipline history & scope
nodes.one_line: Trace ethnomusicology from 1880s comparative musicology (Stumpf, Hornbostel) and Bartók and Kodály's folk-music collecting, through Merriam's The Anthropology of Music (1964) and Nettl's surveys, and place any current research question in that lineage.

nodes.label: Music as culture
nodes.one_line: Explain a tradition's music with Merriam's tripartite model — conceptualization, behavior, sound — and show how a single performance instantiates all three layers.

nodes.label: Defining music across cultures
nodes.one_line: Argue where the category 'music' begins and ends for a given community using Blacking's 'humanly organized sound' and Nettl's cross-cultural definitions, instead of assuming your own boundary.

nodes.label: Bi-musicality
nodes.one_line: Learn to perform a short piece in the tradition you study well enough to play it for a practitioner, following Mantle Hood's bi-musicality program.

nodes.label: RILM literature search
nodes.one_line: Search RILM Abstracts of Music Literature by topic, region, and instrument to find the peer-reviewed scholarship on any tradition in under an hour.

nodes.label: Research questions
nodes.one_line: Turn a curiosity about a music culture into three answerable research questions — descriptive, comparative, or applied — each with the observable evidence it implies.

nodes.label: Disciplinary debates
nodes.one_line: Articulate the emic/etic and scientific/interpretive debates and defend your own position with named practitioners on each side, instead of writing as if the field had one method.

nodes.label: Fieldwork preparation
nodes.one_line: Produce a fieldwork plan — site, duration, contacts, recording kit, budget, and IRB timeline — that a supervisor could execute, before you leave home.

nodes.label: Access & entry
nodes.one_line: Identify the gatekeepers and introduction chains that grant access to a music community, and secure an explicit invitation before recording anything.

nodes.label: Field recording
nodes.one_line: Field-record a live performance with a portable recorder (e.g., Zoom H5) at usable levels and clean sound — no clipping, no wind rumble, no dead batteries — in one take.

nodes.label: Ethnographic interviewing
nodes.one_line: Run a 30-minute open-ended ethnographic interview that elicits a musician's own account of their practice, using follow-up and silence instead of a fixed questionnaire.

nodes.label: Participant observation
nodes.one_line: Attend and participate in a music event without disrupting it, then describe what changed about your access and understanding because you participated.

nodes.label: Field notes
nodes.one_line: Convert jottings made in the field into daily expanded notes with time, place, and people indexed, within 24 hours, so they are usable evidence later.

nodes.label: Transcription & notation fundamentals
nodes.one_line: Transcribe a 30-second recorded passage into readable notation with correct pitches, rhythm, and meter, choosing Western staff notation, LAB shorthand, or a graphical system as the music demands.

nodes.label: LAB shorthand notation
nodes.one_line: Write and read Seeger's LAB shorthand — letter names, accidentals, bars — to capture a melodic line on the fly, faster than full staff notation.

nodes.label: Rhythm & meter notation
nodes.one_line: Notate non-isochronous and additive rhythms — aksak meters like Bulgarian 7/8, West African bell timelines, clave — with tuplets, changing meters, and stroke notation, without forcing them into 4/4.

nodes.label: Tuning & pitch measurement
nodes.one_line: Measure and notate a non-equal-tempered tuning in cents and Hz (e.g., sléndro/pélog, maqam quarter tones) with a tuner or software, and show the deviations from the tempered scale.

nodes.label: Graphical notation
nodes.one_line: Produce a graphical transcription — waveform- or spectrogram-based, using Sonic Visualiser or Praat — for a passage that defeats staff notation, and annotate the features you mean.

nodes.label: Transcription software
nodes.one_line: Use Audacity or Transcribe! to slow, loop, and EQ a recording, and produce a transcription whose tricky passages you can defend measure by measure.

nodes.label: Limits of notation
nodes.one_line: State what your notation cannot show — timbre, microtiming, performance nuance — using Seeger's prescriptive/descriptive distinction, and choose a notation that fits your analytical claim.

nodes.label: Formal musical analysis
nodes.one_line: Analyze a transcribed piece for form, scale, rhythm, and timbre, and write up the analysis with labeled examples drawn from your own transcription.

nodes.label: Scale & mode analysis
nodes.one_line: Classify a piece's scale or mode system — raga, maqam, sléndro/pélog, pentatonic set — from measured intervals, and name the system the tradition itself uses.

nodes.label: Rhythmic analysis
nodes.one_line: Describe a piece's rhythmic structure — metrical framework, timeline, polyrhythm, improvisatory variation — in terms the musicians would recognize.

nodes.label: Cultural interpretation
nodes.one_line: Interpret a musical feature — a mode, a drum pattern, a song text — as cultural meaning (function, identity, emotion) in the tradition's own terms, following Merriam's 'music in culture'.

nodes.label: Cross-cultural comparison
nodes.one_line: Compare two traditions on a single dimension — melody, rhythm, function — with a controlled method like Lomax's cantometrics or a parameter you define, while acknowledging what the comparison flattens.

nodes.label: Emic & etic analysis
nodes.one_line: Separate insider categories (emic) from analyst categories (etic) in your analysis and label each claim, so a reader always knows whose concept is being used.

nodes.label: Performance analysis
nodes.one_line: Analyze variation across performances of the 'same' piece — ornamentation, microtiming, improvisation — and account for it as performance practice, not error.

nodes.label: Thick description
nodes.one_line: Write a thick-description passage (Geertz) of a performance you observed — action, sound, context, meaning — from your field notes, dense enough to ground a claim.

nodes.label: Reflexivity
nodes.one_line: Write a reflexive passage positioning yourself — access, biases, relationships, how you changed the room — into the account, instead of writing as an invisible narrator.

nodes.label: Voice & polyphony
nodes.one_line: Compose a passage that represents a consultant's voice — quoted, translated, contextualized — alongside your own analysis, so the two are distinct yet both present.

nodes.label: Ethnographic structure
nodes.one_line: Structure a full ethnographic argument — chapter or article — with an introduction that states the claim, evidence chapters, and a conclusion, so a reader can state your thesis after one read.

nodes.label: Publication venues
nodes.one_line: Match a finished piece of writing to a real venue — Ethnomusicology, Yearbook for Traditional Music, Ethnomusicology Forum, an edited volume — and reformat it to that venue's stated conventions.

nodes.label: Multi-sited ethnography
nodes.one_line: Design a multi-sited study tracing one music across locations — a diaspora community, a festival circuit, streaming platforms — with a method specified for each site.

nodes.label: Informed consent in the field
nodes.one_line: Get informed consent — oral or written, in the consultant's language — for recording, quoting, and archiving, and document refusal when it happens.

nodes.label: IRB protocols
nodes.one_line: Write and submit an IRB protocol for research with musicians — recruitment, consent forms, data security, risk — and address the board's revisions.

nodes.label: Intellectual property & copyright
nodes.one_line: Determine who owns a recording you made — the performer, the tradition, the archive, you — under copyright and cultural-ownership norms, and act accordingly.

nodes.label: Community collaboration
nodes.one_line: Co-design a research or documentation project with community members — shared questions, shared credit, community review of output — rather than extracting data.

nodes.label: Repatriation
nodes.one_line: Return recordings or copies to the community that made them — via archive agreements, community copies, or re-release — and document the return.

nodes.label: Cultural ownership
nodes.one_line: Argue who legitimately decides what can be studied, published, or shown from a tradition — elders, performers, archives, scholars — with named positions in the debate.

nodes.label: Recording metadata
nodes.one_line: Describe a field recording with enough metadata — who, what, when, where, instrument, genre, rights — to be findable and usable, using a standard like Dublin Core or LCMPI MARC fields.

nodes.label: File standards & digitization
nodes.one_line: Convert a field recording into archival file standards — WAV/BWF 96 kHz/24-bit masters, lossless or compressed access copies, checksums, named per a convention — so it survives.

nodes.label: Long-term preservation
nodes.one_line: Store a digital collection so it survives a decade — redundant copies, verified checksums, format migration on a schedule, no single point of failure.

nodes.label: Collection cataloging
nodes.one_line: Catalog a small collection — accession numbers, item-level records, finding aid — so a stranger can locate a specific recording within a day.

nodes.label: Return to communities
nodes.one_line: Deliver recordings back to the source community in usable form — copies, players, community archive, screening — and hand over control of their use.

nodes.label: Legacy collections
nodes.one_line: Triage an undocumented legacy collection — deteriorating reels or cassettes, unknown performers — and set digitization priorities you can defend.

nodes.label: Archive deposit
nodes.one_line: Assemble a complete deposit package — master recordings, metadata, consent and rights records, and the written documentation of the study — and submit it to an archive such as the Archive of World Music, accepted without follow-up questions.
